source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Keep full-length rails raised and increase rounding, because rails remain appropriate fall-prevention barriers even when the client has begun climbing over them.","B":"Pad the rail openings and continue full-length rails without reassessment, because padding alone removes the main entrapment and climbing risks.","C":"Use all full-length rails whenever confusion worsens, because additional rails reduce unsupervised bed exit without creating meaningful additional hazards.","D":"Full-length rails can create entrapment or climbing hazards, so the nurse should assess whether the rails increase rather than reduce this client's risk."}}
source_row.rationale: FDA warns that bed rails can create entrapment hazards, particularly for older or confused patients, and recommends individualized assessment. Option D recognizes that the rail itself may increase this client's risk. Option A assumes a rail remains protective despite observed climbing. Option B assumes padding alone removes the need to reassess the rail. Option C incorrectly assumes that adding more rails cannot introduce additional hazards.
source_row.source_detail: FDA Hospital Beds and Bed-Rail Safety — Bed-rail entrapment/fall hazards and patient assessment: frail, elderly, confused patients are vulnerable; rails require individualized risk-benefit assessment rather than automatic use. Current FDA hospital-bed and bed-rail safety guidance; rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: asepsis, equipment/environmental safety, incident/event prevention and infection-control activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: A confused older adult repeatedly tries to climb over full-length bed rails. Which safety concern should the nurse recognize?
